topics.title: The French Revolution
topics.description: Why revolution broke out in France in 1789 and how it changed ideas about rights and government.

lessons.title: Causes and Outbreak of the French Revolution
objectives: Describe French society under the Old Regime
Explain the economic and intellectual causes of the revolution
Narrate the events of 1789
Explain the significance of the storming of the Bastille
lessons.intro: On the morning of 14 July 1789, an angry crowd in Paris stormed the Bastille, a fortress-prison that stood for the king's absolute power. This event marked the beginning of the French Revolution, which ended the rule of an absolute monarchy and spread the ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity across the world. To understand why the people rose up, we must look at how French society was organised.
sections: Society of estates

Eighteenth-century French society under the Old Regime was divided into three estates. The First Estate was the clergy and the Second Estate the nobility; together they were a small minority but enjoyed privileges by birth, including exemption from paying taxes to the state. The Third Estate, about 97 per cent of the population, included big merchants, lawyers, officials, peasants, artisans, labourers and servants. Peasants made up about 90 per cent of the population and paid taxes to the state (such as the taille), dues to the nobles and a tithe to the Church. Only members of the Third Estate paid taxes to the state.
Crisis and new ideas

When Louis XVI became king in 1774, the treasury was empty because of long wars, including help given to the American colonies against Britain, and the cost of the extravagant court at Versailles. To meet expenses, the state raised taxes. A growing population increased the demand for food grains, but production did not keep up, so the price of bread rose sharply while wages did not, leading to subsistence crises. Meanwhile, the growing middle class read philosophers who questioned privilege by birth. John Locke argued against the divine right of kings, Jean-Jacques Rousseau proposed a government based on a social contract with the people, and Montesquieu suggested dividing power among the legislative, executive and judiciary.
The events of 1789

In May 1789 Louis XVI called a meeting of the Estates General to approve new taxes. Each estate had one vote, so the first two could always outvote the Third Estate. The Third Estate demanded voting by head, one vote per member, and when this was refused, its representatives declared themselves the National Assembly and swore in the Tennis Court Oath not to separate until they had drafted a constitution limiting the king's powers. Paris was in turmoil because of food shortages, and on 14 July crowds stormed the Bastille. In the countryside, peasants attacked manor houses. In August, the Assembly abolished the feudal system and the privileges of the clergy and nobility, and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen.
definitions: The society and government of France before 1789.
A political body with representatives of the three estates.
A tax paid to the Church, usually one-tenth of agricultural produce.
A situation in which basic means of livelihood are endangered.
The idea that government is based on an agreement among people.
examples: A peasant paid the taille to the state, feudal dues to the noble and the tithe to the Church.
France celebrates 14 July as its national day, Bastille Day.

worked.problem: Why did the Third Estate object to the voting system of the Estates General?
steps: Each estate had one collective vote.
The clergy and nobility, who shared privileges, could combine to outvote the Third Estate 2 to 1.
The Third Estate represented about 97% of people but would always lose.
So it demanded voting by head, which would reflect its numbers.
worked.answer: Voting by estate let the privileged minority outvote the majority; the Third Estate wanted one vote per member.

lessons.real_world: The ideas of the French Revolution, especially that rights belong to all people rather than to a privileged few, influenced constitutions around the world, including India's commitment to liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble.

lessons.title: France Becomes a Republic and the Legacy of the Revolution
objectives: Describe the Constitution of 1791 and the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Explain how France became a republic and the Reign of Terror
Describe changes in daily life and women's struggle for rights
Evaluate the legacy of the revolution
lessons.intro: The fall of the Bastille was only the beginning. Over the next decade France tried a constitutional monarchy, became a republic, executed its king, lived through a period of terror and finally came under the rule of Napoleon Bonaparte. Despite the violence and turmoil, the revolution changed political ideas permanently: the idea that sovereignty belongs to the people, not to a king, spread across Europe and the world.
sections: Constitutional monarchy

In 1791 the National Assembly completed a constitution that made France a constitutional monarchy, limiting the king's powers and dividing power among the legislature, executive and judiciary. However, only men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least three days of a labourer's wage, called active citizens, could vote; women, children and poorer men were passive citizens without the vote. The Constitution began with the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen, which declared that men are born free and equal in rights, and that rights such as liberty, property, security, freedom of speech and expression, and equality before the law are natural and cannot be taken away.
Republic and the Reign of Terror

Political clubs became centres of debate; the Jacobins, led by Maximilien Robespierre, drew support from less prosperous groups such as artisans and shopkeepers, many of whom wore long striped trousers and were called sans-culottes. In 1792 they led an insurrection, elections were held with all men over 21 allowed to vote, and France was declared a republic. Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. From 1793 to 1794, Robespierre's government followed a policy of severe control and punishment called the Reign of Terror, in which those seen as enemies of the republic were guillotined. It also controlled wages and prices. Eventually Robespierre himself was executed in 1794.
Directory, Napoleon and legacy

A Directory of five members then governed, but political instability allowed Napoleon Bonaparte, a military leader, to seize power in 1799; he crowned himself emperor in 1804. During the revolution, censorship was abolished, newspapers and pamphlets spread, and slavery in French colonies was abolished in 1794 (though Napoleon later reintroduced it, before it was finally ended in 1848). Women formed clubs and demanded equal rights, led by figures such as Olympe de Gouges, but they won the vote in France only in 1946. The ideas of liberty, equality and democratic rights, and of a nation of citizens, became the most important legacy, inspiring later movements including freedom struggles in colonies such as India.
definitions: A monarchy in which the ruler's powers are limited by a constitution.
A form of government with an elected head of state, not a hereditary ruler.
A radical political club led by Robespierre.
The period 1793–94 of harsh control and executions in France.
Literally 'without knee breeches'; working people who supported the Jacobins.
examples: The guillotine became the symbol of the Reign of Terror.

worked.problem: Was the Constitution of 1791 fully democratic? Give reasons.

Women, poorer men and children were excluded as 'passive citizens'.
So it was not fully democratic, since many people were denied political rights.
worked.answer: No; despite declaring equal rights, it denied the vote to women and poorer men.

France became a republic in 1792; the Reign of Terror followed.

topics.title: India: Location, Relief and Climate
topics.description: India's position, physical divisions and the monsoon climate.

lessons.title: India's Location and Physical Features
objectives: Describe India's location using latitudes and longitudes
Explain the significance of India's location
Name and describe India's major physiographic divisions
Relate physical features to human activities
lessons.intro: India is a vast country with an area of about 3.28 million square kilometres, about 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, making it the seventh-largest country. It lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere, between latitudes 8°4′N and 37°6′N and longitudes 68°7′E and 97°25′E. Within this area are snow-covered mountains, vast plains, deserts, plateaus, coasts and islands, which shape the lives of the people who live there.
sections: Location and size

The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′N) passes almost through the middle of India, dividing it into two nearly equal parts. The southernmost point of the mainland is Kanyakumari; the southernmost point of the country is Indira Point in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The east–west extent is about 30 degrees of longitude, causing a time difference of about two hours between Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat. To avoid confusion, Indian Standard Time is based on the 82°30′E meridian. India's central location between East and West Asia and its long coastline of about 7,500 km including islands, with the Indian Ocean named after the country, have long made it important for trade and cultural exchange.
The Himalayas and the Northern Plains

The Himalayas are young fold mountains stretching about 2,400 km along India's northern border. They have three parallel ranges: the Himadri (Greater Himalayas), with the highest peaks such as Kanchenjunga; the Himachal (Lesser Himalayas), with hill stations; and the Shiwaliks, the outermost range. South of the mountains lie the Northern Plains, formed by deposits of alluvium brought by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems. These are among the most fertile and densely populated regions of the world, producing large amounts of wheat, rice and sugarcane.
Peninsula, desert, coasts and islands

The Peninsular Plateau is made of old, hard crystalline rocks. It includes the Central Highlands and the Deccan Plateau, bordered by the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats; it is rich in minerals and has black soil good for cotton. The Indian Desert, the Thar, lies west of the Aravali hills, with little rain and sand dunes. Coastal plains run along the east and west: the western coast is narrow, while the eastern coast is wide, with deltas of rivers such as the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. The Lakshadweep islands in the Arabian Sea are of coral origin, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal are larger and more spread out.
definitions: The physical features and divisions of a land.
Mountains formed by the folding of the Earth's crust, such as the Himalayas.
A landmass surrounded by water on three sides.
Land formed by deposits at the mouth of a river.
examples: Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m, is the highest peak in India.
The Sundarbans delta is formed by the Ganga and Brahmaputra.

worked.problem: Why does the Sun rise about two hours earlier in Arunachal Pradesh than in Gujarat?
steps: India extends about 30° of longitude from west to east.
The Earth rotates 15° per hour, so 30° corresponds to 2 hours.
Places in the east see the Sun first, so Arunachal sees sunrise about 2 hours before Gujarat.
worked.answer: Because India spans about 30° of longitude, which corresponds to about 2 hours of time difference.

lessons.title: Climate and the Indian Monsoon
objectives: Explain the factors affecting India's climate
Describe the mechanism of the monsoon
Describe the four seasons of India
Explain the distribution of rainfall and the unifying role of the monsoon
lessons.intro: In June, farmers across India watch the sky anxiously for the first monsoon clouds. The monsoon decides whether crops will grow well, whether reservoirs will fill and even how the economy will perform. India's climate is described as a monsoon type: winds reverse their direction with the seasons, bringing a wet summer and a largely dry winter. Climate is the sum of weather conditions over a large area for a long time, more than thirty years.
sections: Factors affecting climate

Climate depends on latitude, altitude, pressure and wind, distance from the sea, ocean currents and relief. Because the Tropic of Cancer passes through India, the south is tropical while the north has a sub-tropical climate. Altitude matters: hill stations are cooler. The Himalayas block cold winds and trap monsoon winds, causing rain. Places near the sea, such as Mumbai, have moderate (maritime) climates, while interior places, such as Delhi, have extreme (continental) climates with hot summers and cold winters.
Mechanism of the monsoon

The word monsoon comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season. In summer, the land heats much more than the sea, creating an intense low-pressure area over north-western India, while high pressure lies over the Indian Ocean. Moist south-east trade winds from the southern hemisphere cross the Equator, are deflected to the right and blow as south-west monsoon winds towards India. The shifting of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) northwards, the presence of easterly jet streams and conditions in the Pacific such as El Niño also influence the monsoon. The monsoon arrives at the Kerala coast around 1 June and covers the whole country by mid-July. It has 'breaks', dry spells between wet spells.
Seasons and rainfall

India has four seasons. The cold weather season (December to February) has cool, dry north-east winds, with some rain on the Tamil Nadu coast and western disturbances bringing winter rain to the north-west. The hot weather season (March to May) brings high temperatures, a hot dry wind called the loo in the north, and pre-monsoon showers such as 'mango showers' in Kerala. The advancing monsoon (June to September) brings most of India's rainfall. The retreating monsoon (October to November) brings clearing skies, 'October heat', and heavy rain to the Coromandel coast and cyclones in the Bay of Bengal. Rainfall is uneven: Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives over 1,100 cm a year, while western Rajasthan receives under 20 cm. The monsoon's shared rhythm of sowing, harvests and festivals unites the country.
definitions: The average weather conditions of an area over a long period.
Seasonal reversal of wind direction, bringing a rainy season.
Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, a low-pressure belt where trade winds meet.
A hot, dry wind blowing over north India in summer afternoons.
A dry spell during the rainy season.
examples: Mawsynram is one of the wettest places on Earth.

worked.answer: Retreating/north-east monsoon winds gather moisture over the Bay of Bengal and shed it on the Tamil Nadu coast.

Differential heating of land and sea, the ITCZ and jet streams drive the monsoon.

topics.title: Democracy and Elections
topics.description: What democracy means and how elections make it work in India.

lessons.title: What Is Democracy? Why Democracy?
objectives: Define democracy and identify its key features
Distinguish democracies from non-democracies
Evaluate arguments for and against democracy
Explain the broader meaning of democracy
lessons.intro: Many countries call themselves democracies, but not all of them are. Some hold elections where only one party is allowed, and some rulers stay in power by force. Democracy is a form of government in which the rulers are elected by the people. But elections alone are not enough. To judge whether a country is truly democratic, we need to look at who makes decisions, how elections are held, and whether citizens' rights are protected.
sections: Features of democracy

First, in a democracy the final decision-making power rests with representatives elected by the people; if real power lies with an unelected army or ruler, it is not a democracy. Second, elections must offer a free and fair choice and the opportunity to change the current rulers; elections in which the ruling party always wins through fraud or force are not democratic. Third, each adult citizen must have one vote and each vote one value. Fourth, a democratic government rules within limits set by constitutional law and citizens' rights, and is answerable to courts, the media and the people.
Arguments for and against

Critics argue that leaders in a democracy keep changing, causing instability; that democracy involves political competition and delays decision-making; that elected leaders may not know the people's best interests; that it leads to corruption because it is based on electoral competition; and that ordinary people may not know what is good for them. Supporters reply that democracy is more accountable because the government must answer to the people; it improves the quality of decision-making through consultation and discussion; it provides a way to deal with differences and conflicts peacefully; it enhances the dignity of citizens because it is based on political equality; and it allows mistakes to be corrected through public debate.
A broader meaning

Democracy is not only a form of government; it is also a principle that can be applied to any sphere of life, such as a family, a school or a workplace. In a democratic family, decisions are taken by discussion and everyone's views count. A direct democracy, in which all citizens take decisions together, is possible only in small communities, so modern democracies are representative: people elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf. A democratic decision involves consultation with and consent of all those affected, and those without power have the same say as those with power. No country is a perfect democracy; democracy must always be deepened.
definitions: A form of government in which rulers are elected by the people.
A system in which people elect representatives to make decisions for them.
An election that offers real choice and allows rulers to be changed.
Each adult citizen has one vote and each vote one value.
The obligation of rulers to answer for their actions.
examples: A country where an unelected army chief overrules the elected government is not a full democracy.
A school student council elected by all students applies democratic principles.

worked.problem: In Country X, elections are held regularly, but opposition parties are banned and newspapers cannot criticise the government. Is it a democracy?
steps: Check free and fair choice: banning opposition parties removes real choice.
Check the possibility of changing rulers: without opposition, the ruling party cannot be voted out.
Check rights: censoring newspapers violates freedom of expression.
So, despite elections, key democratic features are missing.
worked.answer: No; regular elections without free choice, opposition or rights do not make a democracy.

lessons.title: Electoral Politics in India
objectives: Explain why elections are needed in a democracy
Describe the system of constituencies and reserved seats
Describe the steps of an election in India
Explain the role of the Election Commission in ensuring free and fair elections
lessons.intro: Every five years, hundreds of millions of Indians queue at polling booths, get a mark of indelible ink on their finger and press a button on an electronic voting machine. Elections are the mechanism by which people choose their representatives at regular intervals and change them if they wish. Holding free and fair elections in a country as large and diverse as India is an enormous task.
sections: Why elections and what makes them democratic

In a large community it is impossible for everyone to take part in every decision, so people choose representatives through elections. In an election, voters choose who will make laws, who will form the government and which party's policies will guide it. A democratic election has five minimum conditions: everyone should be able to choose, with one vote each; there should be parties and candidates free to contest, offering real choice; elections must be held regularly; the candidate preferred by the people should get elected; and elections must be conducted in a free and fair manner. Competition between parties is sometimes criticised as divisive, but it encourages parties to serve the people.
Constituencies and reserved seats

India follows area-based representation: the country is divided into constituencies, and voters in each elect one representative. For the Lok Sabha there are 543 constituencies, and the elected representative is a Member of Parliament (MP). Each state is similarly divided into Assembly constituencies electing MLAs. To ensure that weaker sections are represented, some constituencies are reserved for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST): only candidates from these communities can contest there, though all voters can vote. One-third of seats in rural and urban local bodies are reserved for women. Every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, and the voters' list (electoral roll) is updated regularly; voters can show their Elector Photo Identity Card.
The process and the Election Commission

The steps include nomination of candidates (who must file details of criminal cases, assets, liabilities and education), election campaigns in which parties present manifestos and slogans, polling, and counting of votes. Elections are conducted by the Election Commission of India, an independent body whose Chief Election Commissioner is appointed by the President but cannot easily be removed. It enforces a Model Code of Conduct, controls government officials on election duty, and can order re-polls. Challenges to fair elections include the influence of money and muscle power, candidates with criminal records, and unequal resources among parties; yet high voter turnout, especially among poor and less privileged groups, and the frequent defeat of ruling parties show that Indian elections are largely free and fair.
definitions: A geographical area whose voters elect one representative.
A constituency where only candidates from SC or ST communities can contest.
The official list of people eligible to vote.
A document in which a party states its policies and promises.
Rules parties and candidates must follow during elections.
examples: Indelible ink on a voter's finger prevents voting twice.

worked.problem: How does reserving constituencies for SCs and STs strengthen democracy, given that all voters still vote?
steps: In open competition, candidates from historically disadvantaged groups might rarely win because of resources and prejudice.
Reservation guarantees that some representatives come from these groups.
All voters still choose among them, so the representative remains accountable to the whole constituency.
This ensures diverse voices in the legislature, making democracy more inclusive.
worked.answer: It guarantees representation for weaker sections while keeping representatives accountable to all voters.

items: Election announced; Model Code of Conduct

lessons.real_world: Voters can check candidates' declared criminal cases, assets and education online before voting. The Election Commission's apps let citizens report violations of the Model Code of Conduct, and campaigns by the Commission encourage first-time and women voters to participate.
takeaways: Elections let people choose and change their representatives regularly.
India uses area-based constituencies; some are reserved for SCs and STs.
Every citizen aged 18+ can vote; candidates must declare their background.
The independent Election Commission ensures free and fair elections.
